Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette:
Tane was fifty-five, a nanny by trade, though he had not worked in months. The trauma that shattered him happened three years ago, while he was caring for the Benson children-twins, aged four. During a routine afternoon at the community pool, one of the boys, Leo, slipped under the water unnoticed. Tane pulled him out, performed CPR, but Leo never regained consciousness. What Tane heard in those minutes-the wet, gasping silence, then the mother's scream-returned to him now as auditory intrusions so vivid he would stop mid-sentence, waiting for the sound to pass. He could not tell the story of that day without losing the thread; the grief rose like a wall, and his words dissolved.

In the weeks that followed, Tane began to see the world differently. He had always prided himself on being steady, protective. Now he believed he was fundamentally weak-a man who should have scanned the water more carefully, who should have known better. This belief infused his every waking moment. He felt less like a person and more like a broken object, a failed guardian. Whenever he saw a child's arm or leg-a small hand gripping a stroller, a toddler's chubby ankle-his stomach clenched. Those body parts were the same shape and size as Leo's limbs. The sight conjured not the boy's face, but the limp weight of him. Tane had come to believe that his own weakness made these reminders unbearable; he saw the limb and immediately thought, I am the kind of man who lets children drown.

His memory of the event, too, was shaped by his negative appraisals. Because he saw himself as someone who failed to protect, the memory came laced with grief so heavy that it blurred his ability to recount the sequence of events. When the auditory recall-Leo's last exhale, the frantic splashing-intruded, Tane did not simply remember; he re-experienced the shame of his inadequacy. And each time he could not explain what happened, the belief that he was weak embedded itself deeper. The memory fed the appraisal, and the appraisal poisoned the memory.

At work, Tane had always been gentle and attentive. After Leo's death, he found himself unable to return to the Benson family-the twins' remaining child, a little girl, reminded him too much of the victim. But it was not just them. Any mention of a parent grieving a child, any conversation about loss, sent him into a fog of silent tears. He began to avoid playdates, then declined new nanny positions altogether. He could not bear to watch a child run across a lawn without hearing the splash and the silence. His divorce, already in motion before the accident, finalised during this period; his ex-wife said he had become unreachable, a ghost.

What finally brought Tane to seek help was a small moment. A neighbour's son, about Leo's age, waved at him from a bicycle. Tane froze, then ran inside and sat on his bathroom floor for two hours, unable to move. He realised that he was no longer living-he was merely avoiding. He feared that seeking help would force him to speak the story aloud and lose himself in the grief again. But he was more afraid of staying trapped in the loop: weak, object-like, forever the man who failed.
